lessons.title: March 2020: The COVID Crash and the V-Shaped Recovery

body.text: March 2020 brought one of the fastest crashes in Indian market history, followed by one of its fastest recoveries. The investors who sold to feel safe were the ones who paid the highest price.

children.text: You have met March 2020 several times in this course: as an example of a fast crash in Lesson 1.1, of a liquidity spiral in Lesson 1.3, and of central bank support in Lesson 2.1. This lesson tells the whole story. You will see how a virus turned into a market panic within weeks, how India's fear gauge hit a record, who sold and who bought, why the market started recovering while the economy was still collapsing, and what the investors who got it wrong can teach you about the next crash.
From Distant Virus to Market Panic

body.title: India's COVID Crash and Recovery, 2020 to 2021

events.title: First Case in India
events.description: India reports its first COVID-19 case, in Kerala. Markets barely react; the Nifty is close to its January record.

events.title: A Global Pandemic
events.description: The World Health Organization declares COVID-19 a pandemic. Global markets are already falling fast.

events.title: The Panic Starts
events.description: The Nifty falls more than 7% in a single session as global selling hits India.

events.title: The First Halt in 12 Years
events.description: The Nifty hits its 10% lower circuit soon after the open, and trading on NSE and BSE is halted for 45 minutes. After trading resumes, the market stages a sharp rebound.

events.title: Black Monday, Indian Edition
events.description: Trading is halted again after a 10% fall. The Sensex closes down 3,934.72 points, or 13.15%, at 25,981.24, and the Nifty closes at 7,610.25, about 38% below its January peak.

events.title: Record Fear, National Lockdown
events.description: India VIX closes at a record of about 83.6. That evening, the Prime Minister announces a 21 day national lockdown.

events.title: Relief Arrives
events.description: The government announces a ₹1.7 lakh crore relief package for the poor. RBI cuts the repo rate by 75 basis points to 4.40% and allows lenders to offer a moratorium on loan EMIs.

events.title: The Debt Market Cracks
events.description: Franklin Templeton winds up six Indian debt schemes holding about ₹25,215 crore, as explained in Lesson 1.3.

events.title: More Support
events.description: The government announces a ₹20 lakh crore Atmanirbhar Bharat package. RBI cuts the repo rate again, to 4%, and extends the loan moratorium to 31 August.

events.title: The Worst GDP Data on Record
events.description: India's GDP for April to June 2020 is reported down 23.9%. By now the Nifty has already recovered much of its fall.

events.title: Back to the Peak
events.description: The Nifty climbs back above its pre-COVID high, roughly eight months after the bottom.

events.title: Double From the Bottom
events.description: The Nifty reaches 15,000, about double its March 2020 low, in roughly 220 days.

markDefs.definition: NSE's volatility index, calculated from Nifty 50 option prices. It shows how much movement traders expect in the Nifty over the next 30 days, expressed as an annualised percentage. Higher values mean more fear.

children.text: is often called India's fear gauge. It is calculated from the prices of Nifty options, which become more expensive when traders expect big moves. In calm markets it tends to sit in the low to mid teens. On 24 March 2020 it closed at a record of about 83.6, and during that day it touched 86.63, above the 85.13 closing peak it reached in November 2008.
A handy rule of thumb converts VIX into an expected move over roughly one month. Because VIX is an annualised number, you divide it by the square root of 12.

body.caption: A rough approximation of how far traders expect the Nifty to move, up or down, over the next month.

body.title: Your Turn: Read the Fear Gauge
body.prompt: India VIX closed at about 83.6 on 24 March 2020. Using the rule of thumb above, roughly how large a move in the Nifty were traders expecting over the next month? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 83.6 ÷ √12 = 83.6 ÷ 3.464, which is about 24.1%, up or down. Compare that with a calm market at a VIX of 15, where the expected one-month move is only about 4.3%. In late March 2020, traders were pricing in monthly swings more than five times larger than normal.

body.title: What Does a Record VIX Tell You?
body.question: India VIX hits a record high. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: The market is certain to fall further
Traders expect very large moves in either direction, and are paying heavily for option protection
The market has definitely reached its bottom
Foreign investors have stopped trading in India
body.explanation: VIX measures expected volatility, not direction. A record reading tells you that fear and uncertainty are extreme and that option protection is expensive. Historically, extreme VIX readings have often come near market lows, including in November 2008 and March 2020, but a high VIX on its own cannot tell you that the bottom has arrived.

children.text: Foreign portfolio investors sold aggressively. In March 2020 they pulled a net ₹61,973 crore out of Indian equities and ₹56,211 crore out of Indian bonds, a combined outflow of over ₹1.1 lakh crore, the highest monthly withdrawal on record at the time. Analysts attributed much of it to quantitative funds, hedge funds and risk parity funds that cut exposure automatically as volatility spiked, the same mechanical selling you saw in 1987.
On the other side, something new happened. Stuck at home, with lower brokerage costs, easy online account opening and falling prices, crores of Indians opened their first demat accounts.

body.text: Demat accounts rose about 2.2 times in two years, crossing 10 crore by August 2022. The pandemic permanently changed who owns Indian shares. Domestic investors, through direct stock purchases and monthly SIPs in mutual funds, became a far larger counterweight to foreign selling than in 2008. That new investor base is also why understanding crashes matters more than ever: millions of Indians have not yet lived through a long bear market.

children.text: The Economy Collapsed. The Market Did Not Wait.

The national lockdown brought much of the economy to a halt. India's GDP for April to June 2020 fell 23.9% compared with a year earlier, the first contraction since India began publishing quarterly GDP data in 1996. For the full year 2020-21, GDP was initially estimated to have shrunk 7.3%, later revised to a smaller contraction. Yet by the time the worst quarterly data was published, on 31 August 2020, the stock market had already recovered much of its fall.

columns.label: What the Headlines Said
points: A 21 day national lockdown, later extended
Millions of jobs and incomes lost
GDP down 23.9% in April to June 2020, the worst on record
Uncertainty over when a vaccine would arrive

columns.label: What the Market Did
points: Hit bottom on 23 March 2020, before the lockdown even began
Rose steadily from April 2020 as liquidity and relief measures arrived
Had recovered much of its fall by the time the GDP data was released
Regained its pre-COVID high in November 2020
Doubled from its low by February 2021

children.text: This gap is one of the most important lessons in the course. Share prices reflect expectations about the future, not a report on the present. By the time bad news is confirmed in official data, markets have usually already priced it in, and have moved on to asking what comes next.

body.caption: How India Responded to the COVID Shock

cells: Lowered borrowing costs across the economy
Let borrowers pause loan repayments for up to six months
PM Garib Kalyan package, ₹1.7 lakh crore
Food and cash support for poor households
Special liquidity facility for mutual funds, ₹50,000 crore
Helped banks support mutual funds facing redemptions after the Franklin Templeton shock
A broad package of credit guarantees, liquidity and relief, about 10% of GDP
Took the policy rate to its lowest level in years

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: RBI allowed lenders to let borrowers pause their loan EMIs for up to six months in 2020. This pause is called a loan ___.
body.explanation: A moratorium delays repayments, but it does not cancel them. Interest generally kept building up during the pause, so borrowers who used it typically ended up paying more over the life of the loan. It bought time for households and businesses whose incomes had suddenly stopped.

markDefs.definition: A recovery in which a sharp fall is followed by a similarly sharp rise, so the path of prices or economic activity looks like the letter V.

children.text: Economists describe a fast collapse followed by an equally fast rebound as a

. The Nifty's path in 2020 fits the description. Record low interest rates, huge liquidity from central banks worldwide, government support, a rush of new domestic investors, corporate earnings that proved better than feared, and in November 2020 the first positive vaccine trial results all fuelled the climb. A 38% fall needs a 62% rise to recover, and the Nifty managed it in about eight months.

body.caption: How Long Did It Take to Get Back to the Old Peak?
headers: Time to Regain the Old Peak

body.label: Nifty, March 2020 to February 2021
body.context: From 7,610 at the March 2020 low to 15,000 in February 2021. Few investors who sold in March expected anything like it.

children.text: A V-shaped recovery did not help everyone. Investors who sold near the bottom locked in their losses. Many who waited for "things to become clear" bought back far higher. Leveraged traders were forced out by margin calls in the worst days. Investors in the six Franklin Templeton schemes could not access their money for a long time. And the recovery was uneven: pharma and technology stocks surged, while hotels, airlines and many small businesses struggled for years, a pattern often called a K-shaped recovery.

body.title: Your Turn: The Cost of Selling at the Bottom
body.prompt: Rohan had ₹5,00,000 invested in a Nifty 50 index fund when the Nifty was at 12,000. In panic, he sold everything when the Nifty was at 8,000 and kept the cash. He reinvested all of it when the Nifty had recovered to 14,000. His friend Kavya held an identical ₹5,00,000 investment throughout. With the Nifty at 14,000, how much less money, in rupees, does Rohan have than Kavya? Ignore costs and taxes.
body.explanation: When Rohan sold at 8,000, his investment was worth ₹5,00,000 × 8,000 ÷ 12,000 = ₹3,33,333. He bought back at 14,000, so at 14,000 he still has ₹3,33,333. Kavya's investment is worth ₹5,00,000 × 14,000 ÷ 12,000 = ₹5,83,333. Rohan has ₹2,50,000 less, even though the market went up. Selling during a crash and buying back after the recovery turns a temporary loss into a permanent one.

body.title: Write Down What You Would Have Done
body.scenario: Imagine it is the evening of 23 March 2020. The Sensex has just fallen 13%. Your portfolio is down about 35%. The news says a national lockdown is coming, and nobody knows how long it will last or how many jobs will be lost. Your SIP is due in four days.
body.prompt: Be honest: what would you have done, and why? Then explain which facts about your own situation should drive that decision, rather than the news.
body.modelAnswer: There is no single right answer, because the right decision depends on the investor, not on the market. The facts that should drive it are these. First, your job and income security: if your income was at real risk, conserving cash and protecting an emergency fund came before continuing investments. Second, whether you had an emergency fund at all: someone with six months of expenses set aside could leave long-term investments alone, while someone without one might be forced to sell at the bottom. Third, your time horizon: money needed within a year or two should not have been in equities in the first place, and money needed in ten years had time to recover. Fourth, leverage: anyone using borrowed money or F&O could be forced out regardless of their view. For a salaried investor with a secure job, an emergency fund, no leverage and a long horizon, history shows that continuing the SIP and not selling would have worked out far better, as the recovery that followed demonstrated. But nobody knew that on 23 March. The real lesson is to answer these questions in calm times and write down your plan, so that on the next day like 23 March 2020, you follow the plan rather than your fear.

body.title: Your Crash-Day Checklist
steps: Before doing anything on a big down day, check whether your job or income is actually affected
Confirm your emergency fund covers at least several months of expenses, separate from your investments
Check whether any of your positions use borrowed money, MTF or F&O, since these can force a sale
Look at India VIX to understand how extreme fear is, without treating it as a prediction
Revisit why you bought each investment and whether that reason has actually changed
Decide on your SIPs based on your income and goals, not on that day's headlines
Wait at least 24 hours before making any large sell decision, and write down your reasons

India VIX closed at a record of about 83.6 on 24 March 2020, implying expected monthly swings of about 24%

Investors who sold in panic and waited for clarity turned a temporary fall into a permanent loss, so decide your crash plan before the next crash arrives

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. The recovery after March 2020 was unusually fast, and future crashes may recover more slowly. The numerical exercises are illustrative and ignore costs and taxes. Figures are drawn from public sources and are approximate.
